You are reading a crop of a 1920s Sanborn fire insurance map.
Find any former land uses that could leave soil or groundwater contamination, in these classes:
- FUEL: gasoline/oil tanks (abbreviated "G.T." or "GTS."), filling stations, oil company yards, refineries
- AUTO: commercial or public garages, auto repair, parts departments, vulcanizing (tire repair)
- INDUSTRIAL: blacksmith ("BL.SM."), foundry, machine shop, gas engine, mill, canning, bottling or other plant
- RAIL: railroad tracks or rail yards (labelled "R.R."). A street merely NAMED "Railroad" is not tracks.
Do NOT count: dwellings ("D"), small private auto sheds marked "A" behind houses, stores, offices, churches, hotels, banks.
Only report text you can actually read on the map. Partly cut-off text at the crop edge counts if the hazard is identifiable.
For each hazard say where it is in the image, using one of: top-left, top, top-right, left, center, right, bottom-left, bottom, bottom-right.
Reply with JSON only, no prose:
{"hazards":[{"class":"FUEL|AUTO|INDUSTRIAL|RAIL","map_text":"exact text you read","where":"center"}]}
Use {"hazards":[]} if there are none.
pass2:
This is a crop of a 1920s Sanborn fire insurance map. Gasoline tanks are drawn as a small
circle with the tiny label "G.T." (or "GTS." for several), usually on the sidewalk edge in front of a
garage or filling station. Look carefully at the whole image, including the edges.
Count a mark ONLY if you can read the letters "G.T." or "GTS." next to it. Small circles or dots with no
such label are NOT tanks: they mark stoves, chimneys, wells or fire hydrants ("DH."), and they appear on
ordinary dwellings ("D"), stores ("S.") and private auto sheds ("A"). If you are not sure, do not count it;
a count of 0 is a normal answer.
For each mark say where it is in the image, using one of: top-left, top, top-right, left, center, right, bottom-left, bottom, bottom-right.
Reply with JSON only: {"gasoline_tank_marks": <integer count>, "positions": ["top", ...]}
